title: What Does ‘Meets Expectations’ Mean, Anyway?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note argues that the common performance-review verdict of meets expectations sounds like a standard but is not one, because expectations live in a single leader's head and differ from team to team. It cites a study of more than 4,000 managers in which the raters' own tendencies explained more than half of the variance in ratings while actual performance explained only about a fifth to a quarter. The vague label spares the leader a hard conversation, leaves the team member nothing to act on and cannot separate a solid performer from someone coasting. Gallup data show few team members find reviews inspiring or accurate. Adding more rating points does not help, since accuracy levels off around seven categories. The piece recommends a shared frame of reference, a scale anchored with plain descriptors and real examples of concrete performance, so that excellence becomes visible.
points: Meets expectations measures the work against whatever the rater happened to expect, so it reveals more about the leader than about the performance.
In a study of more than 4,000 managers, rater idiosyncrasy explained over half the rating variance while actual performance explained about a fifth to a quarter.
The label lets a leader avoid a hard performance conversation and gives the team member nothing to act on.
Adding decimal precision or more rating points just adds noise, since accuracy levels off around seven categories.
Anchoring a simple scale with concrete descriptors and examples gives raters a shared frame of reference and makes excellence recognizable.
quotes: The words sound like they set a standard, but they don’t. Whose expectations? Set when and written where?
That’s because expectations are leader-specific. They live in one person’s head, and they are a lousy substitute for goals, standards, or objectives.
The managers’ actual performance explained only about a fifth to a quarter.
A rating of “meets expectations” tells you more about the leader than about the work.
A designation of “meets expectations” spares the leader from a hard conversation about performance and leaves the team member without anything to act on.

Studies of rating scales find gains in accuracy level off around seven categories, and reliability begins to slip past 10. A 3.4 that “meets expectations” is still an undefined standard, just with a decimal point.
The job of a rating system is to make excellence concrete enough that people can recognize it. “Meets expectations” asks people to hit a target no one can see.
